definition: The branch of chemistry that studies carbon-containing compounds, particularly those found in living things and derived from crude oil.
A compound containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms. Examples include methane, ethane, and propane.
A mixture of hydrocarbons formed from the remains of marine organisms over millions of years under high pressure and temperature. It is a finite, non-renewable resource.

The process used to separate crude oil into fractions based on different boiling points. Hydrocarbons with shorter chains have lower boiling points and are collected higher up the fractionating column.
A group of hydrocarbon molecules with similar chain lengths and boiling points, separated from crude oil by fractional distillation.
A saturated hydrocarbon with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. All carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds. Examples: methane (CH₄), ethane (C₂H₆), propane (C₃H₈).
A hydrocarbon in which all carbon atoms are joined by single C-C bonds. No more hydrogen atoms can be added.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one C=C double bond. General formula: CₙH₂ₙ. Examples: ethene (C₂H₄), propene (C₃H₆).
A hydrocarbon that contains at least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C). More hydrogen can be added across the double bond.
A family of compounds with the same general formula and functional group, similar chemical properties, and properties that change gradually as chain length increases.
The reaction of a fuel with oxygen. Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot).
Combustion that occurs when there is insufficient oxygen, producing carbon monoxide (toxic) and/or carbon particles (soot) instead of CO₂.
The process of breaking down long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful molecules such as alkenes and alkanes, using heat and a catalyst (catalytic cracking) or steam (steam cracking).
A type of cracking that uses a zeolite catalyst and high temperature to break long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter molecules.
A type of cracking that uses high temperature steam to break long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter molecules including ethene.
A reaction in which atoms are added across a double bond in an alkene, converting it to a saturated compound. Examples include hydrogenation, halogenation, and hydration.
The process in which many small alkene monomers join together through their double bonds to form a long-chain polymer. No other products are formed.
A very large molecule made up of many repeating monomer units joined together. Examples include poly(ethene) from ethene and poly(propene) from propene.
A small molecule with a double bond that can join with many others in addition polymerisation to form a polymer.
A test used to distinguish alkanes from alkenes. Alkenes decolourise bromine water (orange to colourless) because they react across the double bond; alkanes do not.
An organic compound containing the functional group -OH (hydroxyl group). General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH. Examples: methanol, ethanol, propanol.
The alcohol found in alcoholic drinks, with the formula C₂H₅OH. Can be produced by fermentation of sugars or by hydration of ethene.
The process by which yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide in the absence of oxygen. Glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
An organic compound containing the functional group -COOH (carboxyl group). General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH. Examples: methanoic acid, ethanoic acid.
A compound formed by the reaction of an alcohol with a carboxylic acid. Esters have pleasant fruity smells and are used in perfumes and flavourings.
A type of polymerisation in which monomers join together and release small molecules (such as water) as a by-product. Produces polymers such as nylon and polyester.
A synthetic polymer made by condensation polymerisation of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid. Used in clothing, ropes, and engineering components.
A synthetic polymer made by condensation polymerisation of a diol and a dicarboxylic acid. Used in clothing and plastic bottles (PET).
